title: Advances in New Approach Methodologies at FDA's Division of Applied Regulatory Science
nam_sub_category: Standard 2D/primary cells (hiPSC-CM MEA; hiPSC-derived neural networks MEA; cardiac ion channel patch clamp); Microphysiological system (MPS) (small airway/pulmonary permeability; GI intestinal transport); Organ-on-chip (cardiac); QSP (opioid overdose); QSAR ((Q)SAR toxicity and DDI prediction); Other in silico (multi-omics: proteomics/miRNA PD biomarkers)
cou: Other: mini-review of FDA DARS NAM portfolio across multiple COUs - proarrhythmia risk prediction (CiPA/ICH S7B); opioid overdose reversal strategy and naloxone dosing incl. pediatric (QSP); mutagenic impurity (ICH M7) and DDI prediction ((Q)SAR); pulmonary and intestinal drug permeability/transport (MPS); PD biomarker discovery (omics); opioid agonist/antagonist pharmacology (neural MEA)
credibility: Compared with clinical data; Compared with other in vitro data; Regulatory acceptance
contributor_comments: Mini-review of DARS in silico and in vitro NAMs. Table 1 grades each NAM on COU, regulatory maturity and limitations: none is standalone; 'Supportive' = (Q)SAR for mutagenic impurities (routine under ICH M7), QSP opioid model (informed review of submissions and a citizen-petition response), patch clamp and hiPSC-CM assays (CiPA/ICH S7B); 'Exploratory' = small-airway MPS, GI models, hiPSC neural networks, omics. Key limitations: hiPSC-CM maturity and line/lab variability; QSP assumptions on receptor binding/cardiopulmonary physiology and population variability. DARS selection criteria: scientific plausibility, human-relevant biology, standardization/reproducibility feasibility, alignment with CDER regulatory needs. Recommends sponsors submit NAM data alongside traditional endpoints in INDs/NDAs for prospective co-validation vs clinical outcomes; standardized data reporting flagged as harmonization priority. WG relevance: good catalogue of FDA-internal in silico/in vitro case studies (QSP opioid and CiPA are strong case-study candidates); companion to Florian et al. 2026 (PMID 42757693).

title: Advancing Regulatory Adoption of New Approach Methodologies

cou: Policy/Framework: CDER regulatory perspective on what limits and what drives regulatory adoption of NAMs - internal infrastructure and expertise, qualification (ISTAND/DDT), interdisciplinary review teams, guidance development and stakeholder engagement
contributor_comments: Perspective (no new data). CDER has advanced NAMs for ~2 decades; adoption lags the science because of scientific, technical and regulatory challenges that limit reviewers' ability to assess submitted NAMs and advise sponsors. Describes CDER building organizational infrastructure/internal expertise, qualification programs and interdisciplinary review teams, and continued input to NAM developers/end users; NAM submissions to CDER on track to increase again in 2026. Cites draft guidances: General Considerations for the Use of NAMs in Drug Development (Mar 2026; COU, human biological relevance, technical characterization, fit-for-purpose), Monoclonal Antibodies: Streamlined Nonclinical Safety Studies (WoE can replace some NHP studies), and a QSP-based guidance. Encourages early engagement via Pre-IND and INTERACT meetings. Credibility field N/A (policy perspective). WG relevance: useful framing of regulatory barriers/enablers for the landscape intro; companion to Blinova et al. 2026 (PMID 42687608). Could not access full text - verify QSP guidance title.

title: Secondary Pharmacology Targets for Pediatric Developmental Safety Assessment of New Drugs: Clinical Pharmacology Considerations
nam_sub_category: Other in vitro (secondary pharmacology off-target binding/functional assay panels); Other in silico (data-mined target-adverse effect associations for developmental targets)
cou: Safety - chronic: screen new drugs against a panel of pediatric developmental secondary pharmacology targets to flag off-target risk to pediatric development and inform WoE in pediatric study plans, potentially reducing juvenile animal studies
contributor_comments: Found via ASCPT Journal Family LinkedIn post (urn:li:activity:7513674586237026304). Review/perspective proposing secondary pharmacology (off-target screening, routinely run by industry) as a NAM for pediatric developmental safety. Proposes 12 pediatric developmental targets: 7 developmental-toxicity receptors from Lynch et al. 2017 + thalidomide targets + 4 targets identified computationally by N. Tatonetti. Two of the six juvenile-tox WoE criteria could be answered with a pediatric-specific secondary pharmacology panel. Gaps: target list literature-based, no prospective validation against pediatric outcomes; exposure margins and target expression vary by developmental stage. Related: Burckart et al. 'Pediatric Developmental Safety Assessment: Are We Ready for the Next Thalidomide?' (CPT, doi:10.1002/cpt.70148); Abulwerdi et al. FDA/Triangle CERSI workshop report on pediatric developmental safety and NAMs (CPT, Oct 2026); Acitores Cortina et al. BioMADE ML for pediatric screening targets (CPT, Nov 2026, doi:10.1002/cpt.70555). WG relevance: pediatric/juvenile tox is a NAM gap area; possible case study linking in vitro panels with in silico target prioritization.

title: Pediatric Developmental Safety Assessment: Are We Ready for the Next Thalidomide?
nam_category: In vitro; In silico; In chemico; Policy/Framework
nam_sub_category: Other in vitro (secondary pharmacology binding/functional target panels; CRBN binding assay); Other in silico (in silico target binding models; data mining of pediatric adverse event resources); QSAR; ML/AI; QSP
organ_system: Multi-organ (pediatric growth and development; limb/skeletal development as thalidomide case)
cou: Safety - chronic: identify methods that can answer the ICH E11A pediatric safety-extrapolation questions and flag a drug's potential for developmental toxicity in children before pediatric exposure, without building a dedicated pediatric developmental toxicity test system
contributor_comments: Perspective, no new data; the anchor piece of the FDA pediatric developmental safety trio. Argument: pediatric drug development has studied >1,000 products in 20 years but has largely overlooked drug effects on developmental processes, and we still could not predict a thalidomide-type event today. ICH E11A poses 8 safety-related questions but gives no methodology; Figure 1 maps each question to candidate methods (QSAR/chemical structure, secondary pharmacology targets, existing pediatric adverse-event knowledge, ML/AI, QSP). Thalidomide used as the worked case: mechanism traced to CRBN binding and consequent SALL4 degradation; CRBN already has binding assays and could sit in a panel, while transcription factors such as SALL4 are hard to assay, so in silico binding models and predictive algorithms are proposed to cover them. Notes >700 secondary pharmacology targets have been screened and submitted to FDA vs the ~44-target Bowes panel, so the infrastructure exists; what is missing is an agreed list of developmentally relevant targets. Gaps: no validated target list at time of writing, no prospective validation, species-specificity of thalidomide shows why juvenile animal studies alone are risky. WG relevance: concise framing of the pediatric developmental safety NAM gap and of the 'reuse adult-population methods' strategy; good intro citation. Direct companions in this log: Burckart et al. secondary pharmacology targets (PMID 42693525), FDA/Triangle CERSI workshop report (PMID 42823916), Acitores Cortina et al. BioMADE pediatric targets (doi:10.1002/cpt.70555). PMID not confirmed - DOI used as identifier; verify PMID and that SALL4/CRBN details are as summarized if citing specifics.

title: Pediatric Developmental Safety Assessment and New Approach Methodologies: US FDA/Triangle CERSI Workshop Report
nam_sub_category: Other in vitro (secondary pharmacology target panels); Microphysiological system (MPS); Organ-on-chip; QSP (DILIsym for pediatric DILI); PBPK; Other in silico (developmental multi-omics: proteomics/metabolomics-informed scaling; developmental gene expression atlases incl. pediatric GTEx); ML/AI (data-driven secondary target identification)
organ_system: Multi-organ (liver; CNS; developing organ systems generally)
cou: Safety - chronic: use fit-for-purpose NAMs within a weight-of-evidence package to answer the ICH S11 / E11A pediatric developmental safety questions, so juvenile animal studies are run only where they close a defined evidence gap
contributor_comments: Report of the FDA/Triangle CERSI hybrid workshop held Dec 5, 2025 (organizers Burckart, Cuff, Daniels, Meta, Watkins; agenda at trianglecersi.org and FDA media/188215); regulators, academia and industry. Three topics: (i) secondary pharmacology screening tools, (ii) non-clinical tools, (iii) computational and data-driven tools, all framed against ICH S11 and E11A and their question-based approach to extrapolation. Position: historically juvenile animal studies were the sole nonclinical route, agencies now want animal reduction, so the recommendation is question-driven - keep JAS where they answer a defined gap, add NAMs where fit for purpose, with assumptions and uncertainty stated. Specific threads worth mining: making secondary targets routine in development and pediatric-specific target panels built by integrating drug-target interaction data with developmental gene expression (Tatonetti); MPS for pediatric developmental efficacy and safety (Hickman); DILIsym as a QSP tool for pediatric safety analysis (Watkins); a secondary-pharmacology-based tool to flag off-target interactions of pediatric concern (Redfern, Certara); omics-informed modeling of pediatric disposition and safety (Prasad); PBPK and QSP named as the key translation layer, incorporating developmental physiology, enzyme ontogeny and organ maturation; MPRINT data/model knowledge resources for prior information (Li). Conclusion is promise plus need for standardized reporting and better aggregation of secondary pharmacology data. Credibility field N/A (workshop report, no new validation). WG relevance: the single best map of the pediatric developmental safety NAM landscape and of who is working on what; DILIsym pediatric application and the pediatric secondary target panel are both plausible WG case studies; also cites Burckart et al. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2026 (doi:10.1002/bcp.70393) on E11A safety extrapolation, worth adding separately. Full text not accessed - session-level detail above is from the published agenda and abstract/section headings; verify attributions before quoting.

title: Identifying Pediatric and Developmental Screening Targets With Biologically Informed Molecular Representations
nam_sub_category: ML/AI (BioMADE biologically informed molecular representations); Other in silico (pharmacovigilance signal mining across developmental stages; drug-target and gene-level association analysis)
organ_system: Multi-organ (6 system organ classes; respiratory and congenital disorders highlighted in early life)
cou: Safety - chronic: prioritize secondary pharmacology targets whose modulation matters at specific pediatric developmental stages, to compose pediatric-specific safety screening panels for candidate drugs
credibility: Internal/cross-validation only; Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: The method paper behind the Tatonetti contribution to the FDA pediatric secondary-target work. Motivation: >75% of FDA-approved drugs lack pediatric dosing/efficacy/safety data and ~40% of pediatric prescribing is off-label. Approach: extends the authors' BioMADE model (biologically informed molecular representations, originally validated on Torsades de Pointes prediction - AUROC 0.89 internal, 0.74 on the ADMEThyst validation set vs 0.72 for ADMEThyst, 0.77 combined; preprint doi:10.64898/2026.05.06.723121) to find screening targets whose relevance is stage-specific. Data: 3.8M drug-condition records from KidSIDES (the lab's FAERS-derived pediatric signal database, built on 264,453 pediatric reports; browsable via PDSportal) across 7 developmental stages and 6 system organ classes. Findings: univariate analysis recovers biologically coherent genes for pediatric conditions (GABRB1, SLC6A1, GRIN2A - all established developmental/epileptic encephalopathy genes), which serves as the face-validity check; it then nominates secondary targets plausibly affecting development and pediatric-specific ADEs, many absent from current screening panels, with emphasis on respiratory and congenital disorders in early life. Code: github.com/tatonetti-lab/secondary-pediatric-targets (MIT). Gaps/caveats: KidSIDES signals are disproportionality signals from spontaneous reports, unvalidated and confounded (indication, off-label use, reporting bias); no prospective experimental confirmation that nominated targets are pharmacologically engageable or that engagement produces developmental harm; validation is internal plus literature concordance, no clinical or in vivo benchmark; stage-specific expression and exposure margins not integrated. WG relevance: the clearest in silico-to-in vitro bridge in the pediatric set - computational target prioritization feeding an in vitro panel is an attractive hybrid case study, and the honest limitation (signal mining cannot establish causality) is a good illustration of credibility-framework needs for ML-derived NAMs. Full text not accessed - abstract and reference-level detail only; verify target list, model specifics and any performance metrics for this pediatric application before citing numbers.

title: In Silico Clinical Trials in Drug Development: Virtual Patients, Applications, and Regulatory Convergence
nam_sub_category: Other in silico (virtual patients/virtual cohorts; in silico clinical trials; patient-specific digital twins; compartmental to whole-organ anatomical models); QSP; PBPK
organ_system: Multi-organ (cardiac and hepatic most mature; other organ systems earlier stage)
cou: Other: review of in silico clinical trials across COUs - simulating interventions in virtual cohorts to support safety and efficacy assessment, plus the regulatory pathway for risk-informed model credibility
contributor_comments: Review (Balmus, ..., Niederer; Imperial College London/Stanford), Clin Pharmacol Ther 2026;120(5):1181-1194, doi:10.1002/cpt.70492, PMCID PMC13617259. Three contributions: (1) a common taxonomy for virtual patients/in silico trials along two axes - degree of personalization (fully synthetic populations -> hybrid cohorts -> patient-specific digital twins) and level of abstraction (compartment models -> whole-organ anatomical models); (2) survey of applications by organ system, with cardiac and hepatic safety/efficacy relatively mature and other areas still at model-development stage; (3) regulatory history 2008-2026 described as two converging trajectories, moving toward risk-informed credibility assessment and recent harmonization of MIDD guidance. Conclusion: personalized modeling and regulatory pathways often do not yet converge in a unified framework; wider adoption needs robust validation against experimental and clinical evidence. WG relevance: the taxonomy is a useful scaffold for classifying in silico NAMs in the landscape, and the regulatory timeline could feed the landscape intro. Full text not accessed (PMC blocked) - summary from abstract; verify which credibility frameworks (e.g., V&V40, ICH M15) and case studies are covered before citing specifics; therapeutic area/modality fields are best guesses.

title: An In Silico-In Vitro Framework for Model-Informed Precision Dosing in Oncology: Proof-of-Principle for Doxorubicin in Patient-Derived Sarcoma Spheroids
nam_sub_category: Spheroid/3D culture (patient-derived soft-tissue rhabdoid myosarcoma spheroids; long-term exposure); PBPK (individualized doxorubicin PBPK model)
cou: Dose selection: use an individualized PBPK model to translate candidate dosing regimens into tumor-relevant exposure profiles tested in patient-derived spheroids, to identify doses that keep efficacy while lowering systemic toxicity (model-informed precision dosing)
credibility: Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: Dorn, Freitas, Manser, Weidmann, Oehme, Peterziel, Witt, Kelm, Kuepfer; Clin Transl Sci 2026;19(11):e70774 (published online Nov 17, 2026; PMID not yet assigned - DOI used as identifier). Proof-of-principle combining a PBPK model of doxorubicin individualized to a 16-year-old female patient with long-term in vitro testing in her patient-derived rhabdoid myosarcoma spheroids, spanning long low-concentration to short high-concentration exposures. Key findings: response driven mainly by DOX concentration, exposure time nearly irrelevant; inhibitory effect saturated while AUC rose linearly with dose, suggesting lower doses could give similar efficacy with less systemic toxicity. Gaps: single patient/single drug; no comparison with the patient's clinical response reported in the abstract; spheroids lack immune/stromal context; tumor penetration and cardiotoxicity not modeled. WG relevance: clean in vitro + PBPK hybrid case study for dose selection, with a pediatric/AYA rare-tumor angle; links to the pediatric entries in this log. Full text not accessed - summary from abstract; verify credibility/validation details and add PMID once indexed.

title: A Model-Based Workflow to Benchmark the Clinical Cholestasis Risk of Drugs
nam_sub_category: Other in vitro (14-day repeated-dose human hepatic in vitro assay with time-resolved expression of bile acid enterohepatic circulation genes; likely InSphero 3D liver microtissues - verify); PBPK (physiology-based whole-body bile acid model of glycochenodeoxycholic acid)
cou: Safety - chronic: benchmark and rank the clinical cholestasis risk of drugs and new candidates by contextualizing in vitro gene-expression changes in a PBPK bile acid model and scaling the simulated bile acid response to clinical dose
contributor_comments: Generic workflow combining in vitro and PBPK data: gene-expression changes in bile acid transport/synthesis genes from a 14-day repeated-dose in vitro assay (10 marketed drugs) are fed into a PBPK model of glycochenodeoxycholic acid; the simulated bile acid change, scaled by clinical dose, gives a cholestatic potential per drug. Ranking correlated very well with clinical cholestasis risk from the literature; proposed for benchmarking new candidates and supporting animal-free testing. Gaps: 10 drugs; single bile acid species; ranking rather than quantitative incidence; transcript changes stand in for transporter inhibition. WG relevance: clean in vitro + PBPK hybrid for a DILI subtype; same group as the spheroid-PBPK entry (doi:10.1111/cts.70774).

title: Quantitative Systems Toxicology Modeling with DILIsym to Support Phase 3 Dose Selection for Fezolinetant
nam_sub_category: Standard 2D/primary cells (in vitro hepatotoxicity mechanism assays, e.g., mitochondrial electron transport chain inhibition - verify assay list); QST (DILIsym); PBPK (liver exposure of fezolinetant and primary metabolite)
cou: Dose selection: after transaminase elevations in phase 2b, predict dose-dependent DILI risk (ALT >3x ULN, Hy's Law cases) for candidate phase 3 regimens in virtual healthy and MAFLD populations to support the go decision and dose choice for phase 3
credibility: Compared with clinical data; Uncertainty/sensitivity analysis
contributor_comments: After 9/352 participants had ALT >3x ULN in phase 2b, DILIsym (fed with in vitro toxicity data and PBPK-estimated liver exposure of parent and metabolite) predicted a dose-dependent hepatotoxicity signal driven mainly by ETC inhibition. No ALT >3x ULN predicted in healthy volunteers at therapeutic doses; in a MAFLD population, mild ALT increases above placebo and a single simulated Hy's Law case at 45 and 60 mg QD, removed when mitochondrial biogenesis was included. Predictions informed internal/external stakeholder discussions on phase 3 dose; phase 3 confirmed acceptable liver safety at 30 and 45 mg QD (approved at 45 mg QD). Gaps: single drug; Hy's Law prediction sensitive to assumptions about mitochondrial reserve in susceptible populations. WG relevance: strong QST case study of a NAM informing a late-stage dose decision; links to DILIsym threads in PMID 42823916.

cou: Safety - acute: use KIM-1 measured in a kidney MPS, translated with QSP models, to predict drug-induced proximal tubule injury in patients and identify less nephrotoxic dosing regimens
contributor_comments: KIM-1, the clinical proximal tubule injury biomarker, measured in a kidney MPS as a preclinical nephrotoxicity readout; QSP models used for in vitro-in vivo translation and to identify favorable dosing regimens for one of the tested drugs. Motivation: current in vitro and animal models predict drug-induced kidney injury poorly. Clinical benchmark for the translation not described in the abstract - check full text. title: Quantitative prediction of human pharmacokinetic responses to drugs via fluidically coupled vascularized organ chips
nam_sub_category: Organ-on-chip (fluidically linked two-channel vascularized organ chips: gut, liver, kidney for nicotine; bone marrow, liver, kidney for cisplatin; robotic liquid transfer of a common blood substitute with an arteriovenous mixing reservoir); PBPK (physiological PK model with computational scaling of chip data); PK/PD (cisplatin PD)
cou: PK/exposure: predict human PK parameters (first-pass absorption, metabolism, excretion) and PD from coupled organ chips to inform dosing regimen design for phase I trials
contributor_comments: Fluidically linked vascularized organ chips (robotic transfer of a common blood substitute via endothelial channels plus an arteriovenous mixing reservoir), with computational scaling into a physiological PK model, predicted human PK parameters for oral nicotine (gut, liver, kidney chips) and IV cisplatin (bone marrow, liver, kidney chips); predicted cisplatin PD matched reported patient data. Gaps: two drugs; complex, low-throughput platform; benchmark is literature clinical data. WG relevance: landmark multi-organ-chip + PBPK example and reference point for PK-oriented MPS (compare PMID 40829518).

title: A primary human Gut/Liver microphysiological system to estimate human oral bioavailability
nam_sub_category: Microphysiological system (MPS) (fluidically linked Gut/Liver MPS of all primary human cells: jejunum-derived intestinal epithelial monolayer + primary hepatocyte liver microtissue; simulates oral and IV dosing); Other in silico (mechanistic mathematical PK model to derive organ-specific PK parameters, Fa, Fg, Fh and F)
cou: PK/exposure: estimate human oral bioavailability and its components (Fa, Fg, Fh) in vitro to profile first-pass gut and hepatic extraction of oral candidates
contributor_comments: Gut/Liver MPS made entirely of primary human cells (jejunum-derived intestinal monolayer + primary hepatocyte microtissue) that can mimic oral and IV dosing; tissue function maintained in coculture. Combined with a mechanistic model to derive organ-specific PK parameters and estimate oral bioavailability and its components (Fa, Fg, Fh). Demonstrated with midazolam (CYP3A, gut and hepatic extraction). Gaps: single compound; comparison with clinical values not stated in abstract. WG relevance: in vitro route to Fg/F, key PBPK/MIDD inputs that are hard to obtain otherwise; pairs with PMIDs 31988459 and 27760784.

title: Quantitative Assessment of Population Variability in Hepatic Drug Metabolism Using a Perfused Three-Dimensional Human Liver Microphysiological System
nam_sub_category: Microphysiological system (MPS) (perfused 3D human liver MPS with cryopreserved hepatocytes from 5 donors); PBPK (population PBPK model for lidocaine); Other in silico (nonlinear mixed-effects modeling of drug depletion data)
cou: PK/exposure: quantify inter-individual variability in hepatic metabolic clearance in a liver MPS and translate it into population PK variability in vivo
contributor_comments: Hepatocytes from 5 donors in a perfused 3D liver MPS; depletion of six drugs (phenacetin, diclofenac, lidocaine, ibuprofen, propranolol, prednisolone), metabolite formation, mRNA of 90 metabolism genes and viability markers, analyzed with mixed-effects modeling. Inter-donor CV in intrinsic clearance ranged 24.1% (phenacetin) to 66.8% (propranolol); albumin, urea, LDH and CYP mRNA predicted in vitro clearance. Predicted clearance correlated with in vivo values, and a population PBPK model for lidocaine reproduced observed clinical profiles and variability. Gaps: 5 donors; only hepatic variability considered. WG relevance: shows how population modeling can carry MPS donor variability into population PK.

title: Prediction of hepatic drug clearance with a human microfluidic four-cell liver acinus microphysiology system
nam_sub_category: Microphysiological system (MPS) (LAMPS: microfluidic four-cell liver acinus model with primary or iPSC-derived hepatocytes plus endothelial, Kupffer and stellate cell lines); Standard 2D/primary cells (2D culture comparator)
cou: PK/exposure: predict human hepatic clearance from LAMPS (vs 2D and suspension hepatocytes) for drugs and environmental chemicals
credibility: Compared with clinical data; Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: Hepatic clearance of seven compounds (caffeine, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, terfenadine, tolcapone, troglitazone, trovafloxacin) estimated with the four-cell liver acinus MPS (LAMPS; reproducibility previously confirmed in an inter-lab study) vs 2D culture and literature suspension hepatocyte values. LAMPS with iPSC-derived hepatocytes was more precise than primary cells in suspension or 2D but, like other MPS, underestimated in vivo clearance; an empirical scaling factor and a larger compound set are suggested. Gaps: small compound set; systematic underprediction. WG relevance: credibility data point on MPS clearance accuracy vs precision and value of inter-lab reproducibility testing.

title: Combining mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology modeling and patient-derived organoid testing in MET-aberrant non-small cell lung cancer for high-throughput combination efficacy analysis and personalized treatment design
nam_sub_category: Organoid (patient-derived NSCLC organoids from 5 MET-amplified patients; drug sensitivity); QSP (mechanistic multiscale MET signaling network model covering 16 candidate drugs)
cou: Efficacy: simulate clinical efficacy of combination therapies across dose ranges to support dose optimization in MET-aberrant NSCLC, and integrate PDO sensitivity data to design personalized treatment regimens
contributor_comments: Mechanistic multiscale QSP model of MET signaling (exon 14 skipping, overexpression/amplification) calibrated and validated stepwise on preclinical and clinical data for 16 drugs; used for high-throughput clinical efficacy analysis of combination therapies across dose ranges. Patient-derived organoid drug-sensitivity data integrated into the framework to design personalized regimens for 5 MET-amplified NSCLC patients. Gaps: personalized regimens not tested prospectively; 5 patients; check which data were held out for validation. WG relevance: QSP + PDO hybrid for efficacy and dose optimization; parallel to PMID 37765243.

title: Translational Pharmacokinetic/Pharmacodynamic Modeling and Simulation of Oxaliplatin and Irinotecan in Colorectal Cancer
nam_sub_category: Organoid (colorectal tumor organoids; in vitro antitumor efficacy of SN-38 and oxaliplatin); PK/PD (translational PK/PD model with literature PK, plasma ultrafiltrate platinum and tumor SN-38 as efficacy drivers, virtual patient cohorts)
cou: Efficacy: translate organoid drug-response data into predicted clinical tumor shrinkage, PFS and ORR for oxaliplatin and irinotecan to inform drug development decisions and trial design
contributor_comments: Translational PK/PD model: PK from qualified literature data, PD from SN-38 and oxaliplatin efficacy in CRC tumor organoids, linked through predicted plasma ultrafiltrate platinum or tumor SN-38. Virtual-patient simulations gave similar PFS (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.97-1.15) and ORR (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.00-1.32) for the two treatments, consistent with published trials. Gaps: two drugs with known outcomes; relative rather than absolute response comparison; no tumor microenvironment. WG relevance: practical organoid-to-clinic PK/PD translation template.

title: New insights into the mechanisms underlying 5-fluorouracil-induced intestinal toxicity based on transcriptomic and metabolomic responses in human intestinal organoids
nam_sub_category: Organoid (human colon and small intestine 3D organoids); PBPK (simulation of clinical 5-FU dosing regimens to set in vitro exposures of 10, 100 and 1000 uM); Other in silico (transcriptomics, metabolomics, time-series and multi-omics network integration)
cou: Safety - acute: characterize mechanisms of 5-FU-induced intestinal toxicity in human organoids at PBPK-derived clinically relevant exposures to support organoid use in GI safety assessment
contributor_comments: Human colon and small intestine organoids exposed to 5-FU at PBPK-derived clinically relevant concentrations (10, 100, 1000 uM); readouts: viability/apoptosis, morphology, RNA-seq, metabolomics. Key pathways: cell cycle, p53, mitochondrial ATP synthesis, apoptosis, with tissue-specific effects (colon: small-molecule biosynthesis/transport, mRNA translation; small intestine: Rho GTPase and FOXO signalling) and TCA/oxidative stress changes; multi-omics integration identified E2F1 as the key node. Gaps: mechanistic only, no quantitative prediction of clinical toxicity. WG relevance: example of PBPK used to set clinically relevant in vitro exposures; GI toxicity organoid case.

title: Platform combining statistical modeling and patient-derived organoids to facilitate personalized treatment of colorectal carcinoma
nam_sub_category: Organoid (CRC patient-derived organoids, primary and liver-metastatic, characterized by WES and RNA-seq); Spheroid/3D culture (3D CRC cell models sensitive or resistant to FOLFOXIRI); Other in silico (Therapeutically Guided Multidrug Optimization - TGMO: second-order linear regression with adaptive lasso)
cou: Efficacy: identify patient-tailored low-dose synergistic drug combinations that outperform standard chemotherapy within a clinically relevant timeframe
credibility: Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: Therapeutically Guided Multidrug Optimization (TGMO; second-order linear regression with adaptive lasso) used in 3D CRC models sensitive or resistant to FOLFOXIRI to identify four low-dose synergistic drug combinations, then validated in molecularly characterized PDOs (primary and metastatic). In stage IV CMS4/CRIS-A PDOs, regorafenib + vemurafenib + palbociclib + lapatinib inhibited viability up to 88%, outperforming FOLFOXIRI at clinical doses; patient-specific combinations also outperformed standard of care. Gaps: in vitro efficacy only, no exposure link or clinical outcome; concentrations reported in mM in abstract (likely uM). WG relevance: statistical optimization over organoid data; contrast with mechanistic QSP-PDO approach (PMID 41368576).

title: Emergence of spatio-temporal variations in chemotherapeutic drug efficacy: in-vitro and in-Silico 3D tumour spheroid studies
nam_sub_category: Spheroid/3D culture (HeLa-C3 tumor spheroids; sectioning and apoptosis staining over time); Other in silico (mechanistic spatio-temporal drug-cell interaction model of the spheroid)
cou: Efficacy: explain spatially heterogeneous drug efficacy within 3D tumors and inform scheduling of cisplatin + paclitaxel combinations
credibility: Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: HeLa-C3 spheroids treated with cisplatin and paclitaxel, sectioned and stained over time, combined with a mechanistic drug-cell interaction model. Local effect depended on cell repair probability, intracellular drug concentration and mitotic phase: cisplatin apoptosis scattered throughout, paclitaxel preferentially at the periphery. Combination effect depended on scheduling; starting with paclitaxel was more efficacious. Gaps: single cell line; no PK or clinical link. WG relevance: shows 3D in vitro readouts need spatial/mechanistic models to interpret exposure-response; relevant to combination scheduling.

title: A pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model based on multi-organ-on-a-chip for drug-drug interaction studies
nam_sub_category: Organ-on-chip (multi-organ-on-a-chip with a liver compartment for metabolism and a cancer compartment as drug target); PK/PD (PK-PD model describing the chip)
cou: PK/exposure: predict metabolic DDI and its effect on efficacy - simvastatin and ritonavir inhibition of liver activation of the prodrug CPT-11 (irinotecan) - using a chip-based PK-PD model
credibility: Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: Multi-organ-on-a-chip with a liver compartment (metabolism) and a cancer compartment (target), described by a PK-PD model; tested inhibition of CPT-11 (irinotecan) activation by simvastatin and ritonavir. Model simulations with parameters from single-drug experiments matched co-administration experiments in the chip. Gaps: validation internal to the chip, no clinical DDI comparison; one victim prodrug, two perpetrators. WG relevance: early proof of concept for organ-chip + PK/PD in DDI, a COU where PBPK is already mature - useful contrast for credibility discussion.

title: Quantifying ADC bystander payload penetration with cellular resolution using pharmacodynamic mapping
nam_sub_category: Spheroid/3D culture (GCC-positive tumor spheroids with fluorescently labeled ADC and gamma-H2AX PD mapping); Other in silico (computational tissue penetration/bystander model predictions); also primary human tumor xenografts (in vivo)
cou: Target/mechanism: quantify how far a lipophilic ADC payload diffuses beyond targeted cells at lethal levels (bystander effect) to inform ADC and payload design for heterogeneous tumors
credibility: Compared with in vivo animal data; Compared with other in vitro data
contributor_comments: Fluorescently labeled TAK-164 (anti-GCC ADC, DNA-alkylating payload DGN549) tracked in tumor spheroids and primary human tumor xenografts, with payload followed indirectly by the PD marker gamma-H2AX. The payload penetrated beyond the ADC-targeted cell layer, with distance similar to model predictions; lipophilicity gives moderate penetration while limiting washout. Gaps: single ADC/payload; xenograft rather than clinical data. WG relevance: ADC-specific example linking 3D in vitro, in vivo and mechanistic distribution modeling; fills the ADC modality gap in the log.
